title: AI Summaries of Long Documents: How to Ask for One You Can Actually Use

cards.heading: Say what the summary is for
cards.text: Name the decision it supports and who will read it.

cards.heading: List what must always appear
cards.text: Dates, amounts and conditions a reader would hate to miss.

cards.heading: Ask for quotes and page numbers
cards.text: Exact wording with a source makes checking quick.

cards.heading: Flag gaps, never guess
cards.text: A missing notice period should be reported, not invented.

cards.heading: Check it against the original
cards.text: Someone on your side approves it. Legal documents still need reading in full.

facebook.message:
Got long reports and contracts nobody has time to read?
A summary is only useful if it answers your question. Our latest guide covers how to say who the summary is for, what must appear in it, and how to check it before anyone relies on it. Watch for the key points in the short video.

To read the full article, visit the FinTaxTech website and find "AI Summaries of Long Documents: How to Ask for One You Can Actually Use" in our Blog section.

instagram.caption:
"Summarise this" is a weak brief. A summary only helps if it answers the question you actually had.
Watch for the essentials of asking for one you can trust:
→ Say what decision the summary supports
→ List what must always appear
→ Ask for exact quotes with page numbers
→ Have gaps flagged, never guessed
→ Check it against the original before relying on it
